title: Dignity
hook: The application was reviewed correctly. The applicant did not believe anyone had looked at it.
counterintuition: Consistent decisions and dignified decisions are not the same achievement. A person whose application is processed correctly by an algorithm may still report that no human considered their specific situation; even when the outcome was right. Consistency solves one problem. Procedural justice and dignity are different problems, and they do not solve themselves when consistency improves.
tryThisNow: Think of a major decision your institution delivers to individuals. If no human contact came with it, what percentage of recipients would feel their situation was individually considered? That gap is the dignity cost.
keyTakeaway: Procedural justice is a separate and measurable dimension from outcome accuracy. Improving consistency without attending to the dignity stake produces correct outcomes that feel like being processed, not served.

breakdown.fastRead:
Applicants who received algorithmically generated loan denial letters rated their experience 1.4 points lower on a procedural fairness scale than applicants who received human-communicated denials with identical decision outcomes. Thirty-eight percent of the algorithmic group reported that their specific financial situation had not been considered. Twelve percent of the human-communicated group reported the same. The decision was the same. The process was different. So were the experiences.

Consistency and dignity are different properties of a decision process. An algorithm that applies criteria without exception is more consistent. It does not necessarily communicate that anyone looked at this application, this person, this specific set of circumstances.

A decision can be correct and still communicate 'you are a data point, not a person.' Those two outcomes are separate. The consistency gain does not resolve the dignity cost.
breakdown.deepRead:
Social services applicants who received automated eligibility determination and applicants who received caseworker-conducted determination had equivalent accuracy rates in the comparison study: 87 percent correct determination in both conditions. Processing speed was also equivalent. On the procedural fairness measure, the results diverged. Automated-condition applicants rated the fairness of the process at 3.1 on a 5-point scale; caseworker-conducted applicants rated it at 4.2. Fifty-eight percent of automated applicants said they would return to the office if they needed further assistance, versus 73 percent in the caseworker condition. Thirty-four percent of automated-condition applicants described the experience as 'like being scanned, not helped' in qualitative responses. The accuracy was the same. The experience was not.

Procedural fairness is not a measure of whether the decision was correct. It is a measure of whether the person felt their situation was actually considered. That distinction matters because feeling considered is a separate and valued outcome from receiving a correct decision.

A person whose benefit application is processed correctly by an algorithm is better off than one whose application was processed incorrectly by a person. But that same person often reports lower trust in the institution, lower willingness to comply with future decisions, and lower sense of being treated fairly; even when the outcome is right. The procedural justice research says: being correct and being respectful are not the same thing, and losing the second while gaining the first is a real cost. Research on procedural justice consistently finds that people's evaluation of institutional decisions depends substantially on whether they felt heard, seen as individuals, and treated with respect; not only on whether the outcome was favorable. When standardized processes replace individualized assessment, procedural justice satisfaction falls even when outcome accuracy improves, because the experience of individual acknowledgment is a separate and valued dimension of the decision.

An institution where the people it serves are correct in thinking no one actually looked at their case has a different relationship with those people than one where that belief is wrong.
breakdown.fullRead:
The pilot program's second-year data presented to the service branch's personnel policy board showed the consistency benefit clearly across two dimensions. AI pre-screening of promotion candidates had reduced inter-board promotion recommendation variance by 26 percent across the pilot cohort. Apparent demographic rating disparities had fallen by 18 percent in the pre-screened group relative to the matched traditional-board comparison cohort. These were the program's stated goals: more consistent promotion outcomes and reduced systematic variation in how candidates from different backgrounds were treated. The data at the halfway review had confirmed both goals were being met, and the program had been extended for a second year. By the end of the second year, a third column of data had arrived.

Officers who learned their promotion had been AI pre-screened before board review reported organizational commitment scores of 3.6 on a 5-point scale, compared to 4.1 for officers who completed the traditional board review process. Forty-four percent of the AI pre-screened group agreed that their leadership qualities had been fully recognized in the promotion process, compared to 61 percent of the traditional board group. Both measures declined in the AI pre-screened condition even after accounting for the promotion decision itself: officers who were promoted through AI pre-screening reported lower scores than officers promoted through traditional review. A favorable career outcome did not protect against the dignity cost of the process.

'The system produced more consistent promotions,' the policy director wrote in the second-year review. 'It also left promoted officers feeling less seen as individuals than officers promoted through the traditional process. The 0.5-point organizational commitment gap and the 17-percentage-point recognition gap are real costs, measured across the force, including the officers the process promoted successfully. Both sets of numbers belong in the policy evaluation. The question is not whether AI pre-screening is generally good or bad for the service. The question is whether 26 percent more consistent promotion recommendations and 18 percent less demographic disparity justify those costs across the officer population. That is a calculation, not a policy principle.'

In the most important decision your institution makes for the individuals it serves, does the process communicate 'someone reviewed your specific situation' or 'your data matched a category'? The research on procedural justice says these two experiences produce different trust, different willingness to return, different compliance with future decisions, and different long-term relationships with the institution. Those differences are not sentimental. They are measurable, they appear in longitudinal outcome data, and they are worth calculating before choosing how much of them to trade away for consistency gains.

The technology company's before-and-after comparison illustrated the same pattern in a domain where the dignity cost was harder to anticipate. After implementing automated performance scoring as the primary annual review input, inter-manager rating variance fell by 31 percent. Engineer satisfaction with 'my performance review accurately reflects my contributions' fell from 68 to 51 percent favorable. Engineers' agreement that 'my unique contributions were recognized' fell from 71 to 48 percent. And the engineers with the highest code contribution metrics showed the largest satisfaction declines: the contributors whose work was most comprehensively represented by the automated system had the strongest negative reaction to being evaluated primarily through it. A metric that completely describes a person's work output still does not communicate that anyone saw the person behind the output.

The automation solved the consistency problem in both the military and the software engineering contexts. It also produced a cost in each case that the consistency metric did not capture and that the original implementation proposal had not estimated. An institution whose automated process correctly handled a person's application and simultaneously communicated that no one reviewed it is producing both a benefit and a cost. The benefit and the cost are not competing; they are co-occurring. The calculation requires both.

examples.title: The Thirty-Eight Percent
examples.scenario:
The conference room held two printed reports and Odette had placed them side by side: the decision accuracy comparison on the left, the experience comparison on the right.

Accuracy: both the algorithmic denial letter condition and the human-communicated denial condition had produced equivalent decision outcomes across the matched-applicant study population. The algorithmic system generated its decisions more consistently across equivalent credit profiles.

Experience: applicants who received algorithmically generated denial letters rated their experience 1.4 points lower on the procedural fairness scale (where 5 is highly fair) than applicants who received human-communicated denials with the same outcome. Thirty-eight percent of the algorithmic denial group reported that their specific financial situation had not been considered in the decision. Twelve percent of the human-communicated group reported the same. Future banking relationship interest was 22 percent lower in the algorithmic denial group.

'The algorithm produced the right answer more consistently,' Odette said to the product team. 'It also communicated to more than a third of applicants that no one had considered their specific situation. Those two outcomes are real and they are both ours. The accuracy metric is in the left report. The experience metric is in the right report. The design decision requires both.'

The question the team was asked to resolve was not whether the algorithm was producing correct decisions. It was whether the communication design should include a human element that acknowledged the applicant's specific profile, even when the decision remained unchanged.
examples.whatToDo: When implementing an algorithmic decision communication, measure procedural fairness alongside accuracy in the first year of operation. Track the percentage of affected individuals who report that their specific situation was considered. If that percentage is substantially lower than in comparable human-communicated decisions, treat the gap as a design cost that requires a process element to address, not an adoption artifact that will resolve over time.
examples.whyItMatters: Loan applicants who experience a denial as 'my situation was not reviewed' rather than 'my situation was reviewed and I did not qualify' are less likely to maintain a banking relationship, less likely to return when their financial situation improves, and less likely to trust the institution's future communications. Those differences are measurable costs that the algorithmic communication produced alongside the consistency benefit.

examples.title: Scanned, Not Helped
examples.scenario:
'The accuracy numbers are identical,' Fletcher said. 'Eighty-seven percent correct determination in both conditions. The automation achieves what we designed it to achieve.'

Imogen pulled up the second table. 'And the experience numbers?'

Automated condition: applicants rated procedural fairness at 3.1 on a 5-point scale and return intention at 58 percent affirmative. Caseworker-conducted condition: 4.2 on procedural fairness and 73 percent return intention, with equivalent accuracy and processing time.

'Thirty-four percent of applicants in the automated condition described the experience as being scanned, not helped,' Imogen said. 'That description appeared spontaneously in the qualitative responses. We did not ask for it.'

'We built a system that correctly identifies who qualifies and who does not,' Fletcher said. 'We did not build a system that communicates to applicants that someone considered their situation.'

'And those are two different things.'

They agreed the next design iteration should include a caseworker contact step at the decision communication stage: not to alter the eligibility determination, but to provide the individual acknowledgment signal the automated process did not produce. The accuracy of the outcome would remain algorithmic. The communication of the outcome would not.

'The automation removed something the caseworker was providing that we did not measure as a feature,' Fletcher noted in the summary. 'Now that we have measured it, we can design to preserve it.'
examples.whatToDo: When deploying automated eligibility determination for public benefit programs, separate the accuracy function (which automation can handle consistently) from the individual acknowledgment function (which typically requires human contact). Design a human-contact step at the communication stage, even when the decision itself is algorithmically generated, and measure procedural justice scores to verify that the contact step is producing the individual acknowledgment effect.
examples.whyItMatters: Social services applicants, often in vulnerable circumstances, who experience the benefits process as a scan rather than an assessment are less likely to return when their circumstances change, less likely to comply with program requirements, and less likely to trust future agency communications. An agency that measures only accuracy is leaving the second half of its service quality untracked.

examples.title: The Communication Channel
examples.scenario:
Broderick posed the question to the player development staff before the study was designed: if two groups of players receive the same roster decision through different communication channels, one algorithmic and one through a coach, will they respond differently to identical outcomes?

The study's design separated the communication channel from the decision content. Players in both conditions received identical roster decisions, based on the same underlying performance data processed through the same algorithmic scoring system. One group received their decision communicated by data analytics staff who described the algorithmic scoring results. The other received their decision communicated by their position coach, who used the same performance data framed through coaching language.

The answer to Broderick's question was yes.

Players in the algorithm-communicated condition who were kept on the roster, a positive outcome, reported organizational trust scores of 3.8 on a 5-point scale and development motivation rates of 62 percent. Players in the coach-communicated condition with identical decisions reported trust at 4.4 and motivation at 74 percent.

'The outcome was the same,' Broderick noted in the study summary. 'The experience of the outcome was not. The algorithm communicated: your metrics qualified you. The coach communicated: I saw what you brought. Players responded to the difference even when the decision was identical. The channel is not neutral. A favorable decision delivered through a channel that communicates no one looked at you produces a different response than the same decision delivered by someone who did.'
examples.whatToDo: When delivering career-relevant decisions to individuals through algorithmic or data-driven systems, test whether the communication channel affects the dignity experience independently of the decision content. A parallel communication study with identical decision outcomes and different communication channels will reveal whether the channel itself is producing a dignity cost, and whether a coaching or human-contact communication step would preserve the individual-acknowledgment signal.
examples.whyItMatters: Athletes who receive positive roster outcomes through algorithmic communication channels still report lower organizational trust and development motivation than athletes who receive the same outcomes through human communication. An organization that optimizes for evaluation consistency without attending to communication channel effects is trading long-term player engagement for short-term rating standardization.

examples.title: Twenty-Nine Percent Wondered
examples.scenario:
The conference center meeting room had a rectangular table and the kind of lighting that made everything feel procedural. Allegra had arranged the client satisfaction data in the room before practice leadership arrived.

The algorithmic discovery review had produced the accuracy benefit it was designed to produce: equivalent review quality to attorney-conducted discovery at substantially lower cost per document. The clients whose cases went through algorithmic review did not know which review method had been used.

What they reported: clients in the algorithmic-review condition rated 'I felt my case was individually understood' at 0.9 points lower on a 5-point scale than clients in the attorney-conducted condition. Twenty-nine percent of the algorithmic-review group spontaneously mentioned in satisfaction interviews that they were not sure the attorneys had read their documents, raising the concern without being prompted. In the attorney-conducted condition, 7 percent raised the same concern.

A second design test narrowed the gap substantially. When a partner-level attorney conducted a case-specific meeting to communicate the discovery results, the 'individually understood' score rose toward the attorney-conducted baseline, even when the review itself had been algorithmic.

'The dignity cost is in the process experience, not in the outcome,' Allegra presented to the partnership. 'Automated review handles the accuracy and efficiency task. The human communication step restores the individual-acknowledgment signal the automation removed. The firm can preserve the consistency benefit and reduce the dignity cost by designing both into the process, rather than choosing between them.'
examples.whatToDo: When implementing automated document review for client-facing legal work, include a human communication step that explicitly addresses the client's specific case materials in a case-specific conversation. The meeting does not need to repeat the review's findings in full; it needs to communicate that a senior attorney engaged with the specifics of this client's situation. That communication is the individual-acknowledgment signal that the automated review cannot produce.
examples.whyItMatters: Legal clients who are uncertain whether their attorneys read their documents are experiencing a dignity cost that affects their trust in the firm and their willingness to return for future work. The cost is addressable through process design without sacrificing the accuracy and efficiency benefits of automated review.

examples.title: Promoted and Less Seen
examples.scenario:
Bayard had approved the AI pre-screening pilot with the second-year review date built into the approval: all results, both consistency metrics and experience metrics, before any extension decision.

The consistency results were as projected. Inter-board promotion recommendation variance had fallen by 26 percent across the pilot cohort. Apparent demographic rating disparities in the pre-screened group were 18 percent lower than in the matched traditional-board comparison. Both metrics had been the program's stated goals, and both had been achieved.

The experience results arrived from the second-year survey. Officers who learned their promotion had been AI pre-screened before board review reported organizational commitment scores of 3.6 on a 5-point scale, versus 4.1 for officers in the traditional board condition. Forty-four percent of the AI pre-screened group agreed that their leadership qualities had been fully recognized, versus 61 percent in the traditional board group. The commitment gap was largest among promoted officers: successful career outcomes did not protect against the dignity cost of learning that an algorithm had first evaluated their service record before any human board member reviewed it.

'The AI screening produced more consistent promotions and left promoted officers feeling less seen as individuals,' Bayard wrote in the review summary. 'A 0.5-point commitment gap across the force, including the officers we just promoted, is a real outcome. It belongs in the policy calculation alongside the variance reduction and the equity improvement. The question is whether the board can be redesigned to preserve both: the algorithmic consistency in initial screening and a communication process that restores the individual-assessment signal for officers whose promotions were confirmed by the board.'
examples.whatToDo: When implementing AI-assisted screening for consequential career decisions, measure organizational commitment and individual recognition scores alongside the consistency and equity benefits. If the AI pre-screening stage is producing a commitment gap even among positive outcomes, test whether a communication redesign, a board member acknowledgment step, or a direct officer feedback session can restore the individual-assessment signal without sacrificing the algorithmic consistency.
examples.whyItMatters: Officers who are promoted and still report lower organizational commitment than traditionally promoted peers represent a real and predictable cost to retention and mission engagement over time. A promotion process that achieves greater consistency while reducing officers' sense of individual recognition may be trading a long-term force cohesion cost for a near-term rating standardization benefit.

examples.title: Seventy-One to Forty-Eight
examples.scenario:
You are reviewing the automated performance scoring program's impact data, one year after implementation.

Before: you implemented automated performance scoring as the primary annual review input to address the 31 percent inter-manager rating variance the organization had documented across the engineering population. The consistency goal was achieved: inter-manager variance fell by 31 percent in the first year of operation.

After: you review the experience data alongside the consistency data. Engineer satisfaction with 'my performance review accurately reflects my contributions' fell from 68 to 51 percent favorable. Engineer agreement with 'my unique contributions were recognized in my review' fell from 71 to 48 percent favorable. The decline was largest among engineers with the highest code contribution metrics.

The pattern was unexpected. The engineers whose work was most comprehensively captured by the automated metrics showed the strongest dissatisfaction with the metric-based review. A high code contribution metric does not communicate 'your specific contributions were recognized.' It communicates 'your output was counted.'

'We solved the consistency problem,' the impact summary notes. 'We simultaneously communicated to nearly a quarter of the engineering team that their specific contributions had been replaced by a metric. Those are not the same engineers whose work is best captured by the metric. The review process that improved accuracy equity across the population reduced recognition equity for the contributors whose work is hardest to quantify.'

You schedule a design review to determine whether a manager-led annual conversation, using the automated metrics as inputs rather than as outputs, can restore the individual-recognition signal the automated review removed.
examples.whatToDo: When deploying automated performance scoring for complex professional work, track engineer or professional satisfaction with recognition alongside variance reduction metrics. If recognition satisfaction falls substantially, test whether a structured human-led conversation using the automated scores as inputs, rather than as the primary communication, preserves the consistency benefit while restoring the individual-acknowledgment effect the automation removed.
examples.whyItMatters: Engineers who report that their unique contributions were not recognized in their performance review are experiencing a dignity cost that affects engagement, retention, and discretionary effort over time. The contributors most likely to show this response are the ones whose work is hardest to quantify, which often means the contributors with the broadest organizational impact. An organization that optimizes review consistency without tracking recognition satisfaction is systematically under-measuring the cost the optimization imposed.

questions.prompt: What makes procedural justice and dignity genuine stakes in institutional decision-making rather than sentimental objections to noise reduction?
choices: Dignity concerns are genuine stakes because they reflect the opinions of the most vocal critics of automated systems, whose perspectives affect institutional reputation and public-sector compliance rates across programs.

Dignity concerns are genuine stakes because every institution has a legal obligation to provide individualized assessment for each person whose case is reviewed under applicable administrative due process standards.

Dignity and procedural justice are genuine stakes because they produce measurable outcomes: trust differences, return-intent differences, and long-term relationship differences between institutions and the individuals they serve.
questions.explanation: Procedural justice produces specific measurable outcomes that matter to institutions independent of the legal or sentimental dimensions. Lower trust leads to lower compliance with future program requirements. Lower return intent affects long-term service uptake. These are institutional performance costs, not sentimental concerns, and they appear in outcome data that can be tracked alongside accuracy and efficiency metrics.

questions.prompt: A social services agency's automated eligibility system matches caseworker accuracy at 87% but automated applicants score 3.1 vs. 4.2 on procedural fairness, and 34% describe the experience as 'like being scanned, not helped.' What does this data indicate about the agency's automation approach?
choices: The automation achieves its accuracy goal while creating a procedural justice cost: applicants correctly processed by the system experience lower feelings of individual consideration, a real cost in the agency's service quality and long-term applicant trust.

The 3.1 vs. 4.2 procedural fairness gap is an adoption artifact that will close as applicants become more familiar with the automated system and understand that their data was carefully reviewed during the eligibility determination.

The procedural fairness gap reflects applicant preferences rather than a genuine institutional cost, because the agency's primary obligation is accurate eligibility determination rather than applicant satisfaction with the communication of that determination.
questions.explanation: A 1.1-point procedural fairness gap and a 34% spontaneous description of feeling processed rather than helped are not adoption artifacts or preference signals. They identify a real cost in agency performance: lower return intention, lower compliance with program requirements, and lower trust. These outcomes are measurable and matter to program effectiveness independent of applicants' satisfaction preferences.

questions.prompt: Officers promoted through AI pre-screening report lower organizational commitment (3.6 vs. 4.1) and lower agreement that their leadership qualities were recognized (44 vs. 61 percent) compared to traditionally reviewed officers with equivalent outcomes. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: The gaps will close over time as officers become familiar with AI pre-screening and understand that a promotion board also reviewed their records after the algorithmic pre-screen stage was completed.

Favorable career outcomes do not protect against dignity costs in automated processes; officers experienced lower organizational commitment specifically because the process communicated that an algorithm evaluated their service before any human board reviewed it.

The gaps indicate that officers who prefer traditional board review report lower satisfaction with AI processes regardless of outcome, representing a self-selection pattern rather than a genuine dignity cost of the pre-screening program.
questions.explanation: The finding that promoted officers report lower commitment than traditionally promoted peers rules out outcome-disappointment as an explanation. Officers who were successfully promoted still experienced the dignity cost because the AI pre-screening process communicated that an algorithm evaluated their service before any human board member engaged with their record. Positive outcomes do not compensate for process experiences that communicate categorical rather than individual assessment.

questions.prompt: Why might engineers with the highest code contribution metrics show the largest satisfaction decline when an automated performance scoring system is introduced?
choices: High-contribution engineers are more likely to compare their metric scores to peer scores, and any reduction in relative ranking produces stronger dissatisfaction among engineers who previously expected favorable outcomes from individually conducted reviews.

High-contribution engineers often do complex or hard-to-quantify work that metrics cannot fully represent; a system that evaluates their performance through metrics alone is most likely to miss what they consider most important, and they are most aware of the gap.

High-contribution engineers have strong incentives to prefer evaluation systems that allow individualized performance narratives, making them rationally motivated to report dissatisfaction with any automated system that reduces their ability to negotiate assessment outcomes.
questions.explanation: Automated scoring systems capture what can be measured. Engineers whose most valuable contributions are architectural decisions, mentorship, cross-team coordination, or novel problem framing may have high code contribution counts but also significant contributions that the metric does not represent. A metric-based review communicates to these engineers that the unmeasured work was not part of the assessment. They are most aware of the gap because they are most aware of what the metric misses.

questions.prompt: A law firm finds that clients whose discovery was algorithmically reviewed rate 'case individually understood' 0.9 points lower, but that adding a partner-level communication meeting narrows the gap substantially. What does this suggest about how the firm should design its automation approach?
choices: The firm should eliminate algorithmic discovery review because even a partially addressable dignity cost indicates a fundamental incompatibility between automated document processing and the individual acknowledgment expectations of legal clients.

The 0.9-point gap falls within normal client satisfaction variation, and the additional cost of partner-level communication meetings is not justified by a satisfaction improvement that does not affect case outcome quality.

The dignity cost is addressable through process design: automated review handles the accuracy and efficiency task, while a human communication step restores the individual-acknowledgment signal, allowing the firm to preserve the consistency benefit while reducing the dignity cost.
questions.explanation: The finding that a partner communication step narrows the gap reveals the dignity cost's structure: it arises from the absence of individual acknowledgment, not from the automated review itself. The firm can preserve the accuracy and efficiency benefit of automated review and restore the acknowledgment signal by adding a communication step. This is a design solution that addresses the cost without eliminating the benefit, which is available specifically because the cost is in the communication experience, not in the decision quality.

questions.prompt: Why do consumers who receive algorithmically correct loan denial decisions still report substantially lower future banking relationship interest than consumers who receive human-communicated denials with identical outcomes?
choices: The denial process communicates something independent of the decision outcome: whether the institution evaluated this person's specific situation, or applied criteria to their data. That communication affects trust even when the outcome was appropriate.

Consumers misattribute algorithmic efficiency for institutional indifference, a misattribution that would disappear if lenders provided clearer explanations of how the algorithm reviewed each applicant's specific financial profile during the decision process.

Lower future relationship interest reflects consumers' rational assessment that lenders using algorithmic denial systems do not prioritize relationship banking, a product preference signal rather than a response to the specific denial experience.
questions.explanation: Trust and relationship interest are not determined only by decision accuracy. The denial process also communicates whether someone evaluated this specific applicant's situation or applied a rule to their data. When 38% of applicants report that their situation was not considered, that is not a misattribution: the algorithmic process did not include any element that communicated individual consideration. The trust difference follows from the communication difference, not from a perception error.

questions.prompt: An insurance company proposes automating claim determination to reduce inter-adjuster inconsistency by a projected 35%. The proposal documents the variance reduction but includes no estimate of claimant procedural justice effects. What should a reviewer ask before approving the proposal?
choices: Whether the projected 35% variance reduction reaches a threshold that is actuarially significant enough to justify the implementation cost of an automated adjudication system for this particular claims category.

What the expected impact is on claimants' experience of individual consideration, and whether the proposal includes any process design element to preserve the acknowledgment signal that human adjuster contact provides alongside the consistency benefit.

Whether the automation system has been validated on a dataset that fully represents the insurer's current claimant population, since variance reduction projections from non-representative samples may not generalize to the live population.
questions.explanation: A proposal that documents variance reduction without estimating procedural justice effects has calculated the benefit and not the cost. Claimants who receive automated denials or approvals without any human acknowledgment of their specific situation are likely to experience the same dignity cost documented in other domains: lower trust, lower compliance with future program requirements, and lower likelihood of maintaining the insurance relationship. The reviewer's first question should be about the cost calculation that is missing.

questions.prompt: A benefits agency implements a hybrid determination process: algorithmic scoring for initial eligibility, followed by a brief caseworker call to communicate the decision and answer questions. Compared to fully automated processing, which outcome should this design most directly improve?
choices: Applicants' sense that their specific situation was individually considered, because the caseworker contact provides an opportunity for individual acknowledgment that the automated scoring step cannot communicate.

The accuracy of the eligibility determination, because caseworker involvement at the communication stage allows scoring errors to be identified and corrected before the final decision reaches the applicant.

Processing speed, because separating accuracy work from communication work creates a parallel workflow that reduces total time from application to determination relative to fully caseworker-conducted review.
questions.explanation: The caseworker contact step is specifically designed to restore the individual-acknowledgment signal that the automated scoring cannot provide. It does not change the decision (which remains algorithmic) and does not primarily improve accuracy (which the algorithm handles). Its function is to produce the procedural justice experience: a person who can acknowledge the specific applicant's situation, answer questions, and communicate that the agency engaged with this case rather than processed data.

questions.prompt: A service branch finds AI pre-screening reduces promotion variance by 26% but lowers promoted officers' organizational commitment by 0.5 points. A senior officer argues the commitment data is 'soft' and that consistency and equity gains are the metrics that matter for force readiness. How should the policy director respond?
choices: The senior officer's argument is correct: organizational commitment is difficult to measure precisely, and the 0.5-point difference falls within normal survey variation, while variance reduction and demographic equity are objective metrics that directly affect force readiness.

The senior officer's perspective should be treated as one stakeholder input, and the policy director should commission a broader officer survey before making any recommendation about the program's continuation or modification.

Organizational commitment is a real and measurable cost: it predicts retention, mission engagement, and unit effectiveness over time. A 0.5-point gap across the promoted officer population is a specific cost that the policy calculation must include, because dismissing it as soft is declaring a cost irrelevant without measuring what it actually costs the force in the next three to five years.
questions.explanation: Organizational commitment measured on validated survey instruments is not a soft metric: it predicts outcomes that are directly relevant to force readiness, including voluntary separation rates, mission engagement, and leadership effectiveness. Characterizing it as soft because it is not a roster decision or a variance statistic is a cost-dismissal move, not a measurement critique. The policy director's response should name what the commitment gap predicts in operational terms and add those predictions to the cost calculation.

reviewCards.front: What is the procedural justice finding about the relationship between decision accuracy and the experience of individual consideration?
reviewCards.back: Being correct and being respectful are different institutional achievements. A person whose case is correctly handled by an algorithm still often reports lower trust, lower return intention, and lower sense of being treated fairly than a person whose case was correctly handled by a human. Outcome accuracy does not produce procedural justice satisfaction automatically.

reviewCards.front: What distinguishes the dignity cost of automated decision-making from a sentimental preference for human interaction?
reviewCards.back: The dignity cost produces specific measurable outcomes: lower trust in the institution, lower willingness to return, lower compliance with future program requirements, and lower long-term relationship interest. These outcomes are traceable in longitudinal data and affect institutional performance independently of whether the decision was accurate.

reviewCards.front: Why do positive decision outcomes not protect against dignity costs in automated processes?
reviewCards.back: Dignity costs arise from the process communication, not the decision outcome. A person who is approved or promoted through an algorithmic process still experiences the absence of individual acknowledgment. Favorable outcomes do not change what the process communicated about whether anyone reviewed this specific person's situation.

reviewCards.front: What is the individual-acknowledgment signal, and how can process design preserve it alongside automated decision-making?
reviewCards.back: The individual-acknowledgment signal is the communication that a person in authority considered this specific case rather than matching data to a category. It can be preserved through a human contact step at the communication stage: a call, a meeting, or a personal letter that addresses the specific applicant's situation. The step does not need to change the decision to produce the signal.

reviewCards.front: What makes high-contribution professionals particularly likely to experience dignity costs from automated performance review?
reviewCards.back: Professionals whose most valuable contributions are complex, interdependent, or hard to quantify are most aware of the gap between their work and its metric representation. A system that evaluates them primarily through metrics communicates that the unmeasured work was not part of the assessment, which is the dimension they consider most important.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Identifying where automated or standardized institutional processes impose dignity costs, and designing process elements that preserve the individual-acknowledgment signal alongside the consistency benefit rather than trading one for the other

ifThenPlans.context: When implementing an automated decision system for consequential individual-facing decisions
ifThenPlans.plan: Design at least one human-contact element that explicitly acknowledges the individual's specific situation. The contact step does not need to change the decision to produce the dignity signal; it needs to communicate that a person with authority to explain the decision engaged with this specific case. Measure procedural justice satisfaction in the first year of operation to verify the contact step is working.

ifThenPlans.context: When measuring the performance of an automated decision program
ifThenPlans.plan: Add a procedural justice measure alongside accuracy and efficiency metrics. Ask affected individuals whether they felt their specific situation was individually considered, and track the percentage who did not. That percentage is the dignity cost the program is imposing. If it is substantially lower than in comparable human-conducted processes, treat it as a design cost to address, not an adoption artifact to wait out.

ifThenPlans.context: When stakeholders characterize dignity concerns as soft metrics that should not affect automation decisions
ifThenPlans.plan: Name the specific outcomes that procedural justice satisfaction predicts in the relevant domain: for social services, return intention and compliance; for financial services, relationship retention; for professional evaluation, organizational commitment and voluntary separation rates. If those outcomes are not being tracked, propose adding them before deciding whether the dignity cost is real enough to require a design response.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Identify the most consequential institutional decision your organization delivers to individuals. Write down how that decision is currently communicated and whether any element of the communication explicitly acknowledges the individual's specific circumstances. If no element does, the process is trading dignity for efficiency without having calculated the cost.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when reviewing any automation or standardization proposal for an individual-facing decision process, ask: does this proposal include a measurement of procedural justice effects on affected individuals, and does it include a design element that preserves the individual-acknowledgment signal? If neither is present, add both before approving the proposal.
